final_proof:
Let $I_n$ denote the $n\times n$ identity matrix. We first record the finite-dimensional fact needed below: for a linear map $T:\mathbb F^n\to\mathbb F^n$, injectivity and surjectivity are equivalent. Indeed, if $T$ is injective and $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ is the standard basis, then $T(e_1),\ldots,T(e_n)$ are linearly independent: an equality $\sum_i c_iT(e_i)=0$ gives $T(\sum_i c_ie_i)=0$, whence every $c_i=0$. Since these are $n$ linearly independent vectors in the $n$-dimensional space $\mathbb F^n$, they form a basis, so $T$ is surjective. Conversely, if $T$ is surjective, then $T(e_1),\ldots,T(e_n)$ span $\mathbb F^n$; a spanning list of $n$ vectors in an $n$-dimensional space is a basis, hence is linearly independent. Thus $T(x)=0$, after writing $x=\sum_i c_ie_i$, forces all $c_i=0$, so $x=0$ and $T$ is injective.

Now suppose first that $\mathbf B$ is a left inverse of $\mathbf A$, so $\mathbf B\mathbf A=I_n$. Regard the matrices as linear maps on $\mathbb F^n$. If $\mathbf A x=0$, then
$$x=I_nx=(\mathbf B\mathbf A)x=\mathbf B(\mathbf A x)=0.$$
Hence $\mathbf A$ is injective and therefore, by the finite-dimensional fact above, surjective. Given any $y\in\mathbb F^n$, choose $x\in\mathbb F^n$ such that $\mathbf A x=y$. Then, using associativity and $\mathbf B\mathbf A=I_n$,
$$(\mathbf A\mathbf B)y=\mathbf A\mathbf B(\mathbf A x)=\mathbf A((\mathbf B\mathbf A)x)=\mathbf A x=y.$$
Thus $\mathbf A\mathbf B$ acts as the identity on every vector, and consequently $\mathbf A\mathbf B=I_n$. Therefore every left inverse of a square matrix over a field is also a right inverse.

For completeness, the intended symmetric assertion also holds. Suppose $\mathbf B$ is a right inverse of $\mathbf A$, so $\mathbf A\mathbf B=I_n$. For every $y\in\mathbb F^n$ we have $y=\mathbf A(\mathbf B y)$, so $\mathbf A$ is surjective and hence injective. For any $x\in\mathbb F^n$,
$$\mathbf A((\mathbf B\mathbf A)x-x)=(\mathbf A\mathbf B)(\mathbf A x)-\mathbf A x=I_n(\mathbf A x)-\mathbf A x=0.$$
Injectivity of $\mathbf A$ gives $(\mathbf B\mathbf A)x=x$. This holds for all $x$, so $\mathbf B\mathbf A=I_n$; hence every right inverse is also a left inverse. (The problem's final sentence says "right inverse" twice; read literally it is tautological, while this is the evidently intended symmetric statement.)

Finally, this also proves the equality asserted in the title. If $\mathbf L$ is any left inverse of $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf R$ is any right inverse, then
$$\mathbf L=\mathbf L I_n=\mathbf L(\mathbf A\mathbf R)=(\mathbf L\mathbf A)\mathbf R=I_n\mathbf R=\mathbf R.$$
Thus left and right inverses of a square matrix over a field coincide (and, when they exist, are unique).
